steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on semantic polarization between CNN and Fox News, using a decade of TV closed captions, and whether it forecasts polarization on Twitter. Explain why broadcast TV news matters and is understudied, outline our three studies, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why media language matters for democracy and public perception
- TV news still dominates consumption and partisan segregation
- But polarization research is mostly based on online content; legacy media data hard to get
- Our data and the three studies
- Contributions
- What the findings mean

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Mass media plays a vital role in democratic processes. It influences how institutions operate and how political leaders communicate, and most importantly how citizens engage in politics. It is no surprise that America's two political divides speak different languages, but research has also shown that partisan language in news media has gone up sharply in recent years, especially in broadcast news. This is concerning because news consumption is critical for the public to understand the events around them. According to Agenda Setting Theory, the language the media uses to frame and present current events affects how the public perceives which issues are important. Some people may have the impression that mainstream legacy media is getting less relevant because of the explosive growth of online news through websites and social media. But American news consumption is still overwhelmingly from television, which accounts for nearly five times as much as online news consumption across the public. People think of watching TV news as more "passive" than reading the news, but research shows that people tend to remember televised news better than online news. Also, a recent study that compared TV and internet news consumption found that there are four times as many Americans who are partisan-segregated via TV than via online news. TV news audiences are actually several times more likely to keep their partisan news diets over time, and their sources are much narrower, while even partisan online news readers tend to consume from a variety of sources.

Still, studies on media polarization and the public discourse that follows are overwhelmingly based on online content. For example, even research that analyzes data from traditional news outlets only uses tweets from the official Twitter accounts of newspapers, TV shows, and radio programs, and not the direct transcription of content from these legacy media sources. The reason is that legacy media data (e.g., closed captions), unlike online information, are harder to collect, come in formats that are not compatible with quick pre-processing (e.g., srt files), and are scattered across institutions that have no incentive to share data with academics. So a lot about how mainstream legacy media affects online discourse is unknown. Our analysis of a decade's worth of closed captions from 24hr-broadcast TV news programs from America's two largest news stations is therefore a unique opportunity to show empirically how linguistic polarization in broadcast media has changed over time, and how it has affected social media discourse.

- Our data and studies
  - a decade of closed captions, 24hr-broadcast TV news, America's two largest stations
  - Study 1: semantic differences CNN vs Fox News over last 11 years; NLP method, semantic polarity 2010 to 2020; topics: racism, Black Lives Matter, police, immigration, climate change, health care
  - Study 2: words characteristic of polarity peaks; model interpretation technique; contextual tokens most predictive of how each station discusses keywords in 2020
  - Study 3: Granger causality, does TV polarization forecast polarization among Twitter audiences replying to @CNN and @FoxNews
  - finally: tokens most predictive of keyword discussion on TV vs Twitter, separated by lag lengths matching Granger-causality significance (and vice-versa)
- Contributions
  - framework for semantic polarization between two entities with temporality; prior work = aggregate measure from single longitudinal data dump, misses temporal dynamics; diachronic shifts with contextual word embeddings + temporal features
  - beyond a metric: Integrated Gradients for attributive tokens, language behind 2020 ascent
  - whether/how TV language polarization forecasts Twitter polarity; link not established at-scale before
  - model interpretation for lexical features; which words drive Granger-causal patterns both ways
- Implications

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Mass media plays a vital role in democratic processes. It influences how institutions operate and how political leaders communicate, and most importantly how citizens engage in politics. It is no surprise that America's two political divides speak different languages, but research has also shown that partisan language in news media has gone up sharply in recent years, especially in broadcast news. This is concerning because news consumption is critical for the public to understand the events around them. According to Agenda Setting Theory, the language the media uses to frame and present current events affects how the public perceives which issues are important. Some people may have the impression that mainstream legacy media is getting less relevant because of the explosive growth of online news through websites and social media. But American news consumption is still overwhelmingly from television, which accounts for nearly five times as much as online news consumption across the public. People think of watching TV news as more "passive" than reading the news, but research shows that people tend to remember televised news better than online news. Also, a recent study that compared TV and internet news consumption found that there are four times as many Americans who are partisan-segregated via TV than via online news. TV news audiences are actually several times more likely to keep their partisan news diets over time, and their sources are much narrower, while even partisan online news readers tend to consume from a variety of sources.

Still, studies on media polarization and the public discourse that follows are overwhelmingly based on online content. For example, even research that analyzes data from traditional news outlets only uses tweets from the official Twitter accounts of newspapers, TV shows, and radio programs, and not the direct transcription of content from these legacy media sources. The reason is that legacy media data (e.g., closed captions), unlike online information, are harder to collect, come in formats that are not compatible with quick pre-processing (e.g., srt files), and are scattered across institutions that have no incentive to share data with academics. So a lot about how mainstream legacy media affects online discourse is unknown. Our analysis of a decade's worth of closed captions from 24hr-broadcast TV news programs from America's two largest news stations is therefore a unique opportunity to show empirically how linguistic polarization in broadcast media has changed over time, and how it has affected social media discourse.

In this work, we look at how semantic differences in broadcast media language between CNN and Fox News have changed over the last 11 years (Study 1), what words are characteristic of the semantic polarity peaks in broadcast media language (Study 2), and whether semantic polarity in TV news language forecasts polarization trends in social media discourse and how language plays a role in driving relational patterns from one to the other (Study 3). In Study 1, we use techniques from natural language processing (NLP) to develop a method that quantitatively captures how semantic polarization between CNN and Fox News has changed from 2010 to 2020. We do this by calculating the semantic polarity of how the two news channels discuss topics that are socially important but politically divided (racism, Black Lives Matter, police, immigration, climate change, and health care). Then we use a model interpretation technique from deep learning to unpack linguistically what may be driving these spikes, by extracting the contextual tokens that are most predictive of how each station discusses topical keywords in 2020 (Study 2). To see whether partisan trends in broadcast media language influence polarity patterns in social media discourse, we use Granger causality to test whether and how semantic polarization between the two TV news stations forecasts polarization across Twitter audiences replying to @CNN and @FoxNews (Study 3). Finally, to understand the language that drives the Granger-causal relations in how semantic polarity trends on televised news affect those across Twitter users (and vice-versa), we identify the tokens that are most predictive of how topical keywords are discussed on TV vs. Twitter, separated by the lag lengths that correspond to Granger-causality significance. Our contributions are:

- We provide a new framework to quantify semantic polarization between two entities that takes into account the temporality of how semantic polarization changes over time. Prior research quantifies polarization as an aggregate measure from a single longitudinal data dump, and so it often leaves out key temporal dynamics and contexts around how polarity unfolds over time. Our framework includes temporal fluctuations by computing diachronic shifts with contextual word embeddings that have temporal features.

- We show how semantic polarization in broadcast media has changed over the last 11 years, and we go beyond just giving a quantification of polarization as a metric: we use Integrated Gradients to identify attributive tokens as a proxy for the contextual language that drives the 2020 rise in semantic polarity between the two news stations.

- We address whether and how polarization in televised news language forecasts semantic polarity trends across Twitter. This gives new evidence about how online audiences are shaped in their discourse by TV news language, which is an important link that prior research has not established empirically at-scale.

- Finally, we use model interpretation to extract lexical features from different entities and show which words drive significant Granger-causal patterns in how broadcast media language shapes Twitter discourse and vice-versa. This highlights how language plays a key role in driving semantic polarity relations between online discussions and broadcast media language.

Our findings are one of the first to quantify how language that characterizes opposing media narratives about similar news events on TV can increase levels of partisan discourse online. The results support recent scholarship in communications research, which theorizes that media and public agendas can both influence each other, and that these dynamics can polarize the way the public engages in discourse, which then influences democratic decision-making at-large.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Mass media plays a vital role in democratic processes by influencing how institutions operate, how political leaders communicate, and most importantly, how citizens engage in politics [1]. Although it is no surprise that America's two political divides speak different languages [2], research has also shown that partisan language in news media has sharply increased in recent years, particularly in broadcast news [3]. This is concerning, since news consumption is critical for helping the public understand the events around them. According to Agenda Setting Theory, the language the media uses to frame and present current events impacts how the public perceives which issues are important [4,5]. Despite the notion that TV news consumption is more "passive" than reading the news, research shows that people tend to recall televised news better than online news [7]. Further, a recent study comparing TV vs. internet news consumption found four times as many Americans partisan-segregated via TV than via online news. In fact, TV news audiences are several times more likely to maintain their partisan news diets over time and are much narrower in their sources, while even partisan online news readers tend to consume from a variety of sources [8]. Yet studies on media polarization and ensuing public discourse are overwhelmingly based on online content [9]. For example, even research that analyzes data from traditional news outlets relies solely on tweets from the official Twitter accounts of newspapers, TV shows, and radio programs rather than the direct transcription of content from these legacy media sources [10]. This is because, unlike online information, legacy media data (e.g., closed captions) are harder to collect, exist in formats incompatible with quick pre-processing (e.g., srt files), and are scattered across institutions that lack incentives to share data with academics. Hence, much of how mainstream legacy media affects online discourse is unknown. Our analysis of a decade's worth of closed captions from 24hr-broadcast TV news programs from America's two largest news stations therefore presents a unique opportunity to empirically demonstrate how linguistic polarization in broadcast media has evolved over time, and how it has impacted social media discourse. In this work, we examine how semantic differences in broadcast media language between CNN and Fox News have evolved over the last 11 years (Study 1), what words are characteristic of the semantic polarity peaks in broadcast media language (Study 2), and whether semantic polarity in TV news language forecasts polarization trends in social media discourse, as well as how language plays a role in driving relational patterns from one to the other (Study 3). - We provide a novel framework for quantifying semantic polarization between two entities that considers the temporality of how semantic polarization evolves over time. Prior research that quantifies polarization as an aggregate measure from a single longitudinal data dump often leaves out key temporal dynamics and contexts around how polarity unfolds across time. - In showing how semantic polarization in broadcast media has evolved over the last 11 years, we go beyond a mere quantification of polarization as a metric, using Integrated Gradients to identify attributive tokens as a proxy for the contextual language that drives the 2020 ascent in semantic polarity between the two news stations.

- We address whether and how polarization in televised news language forecasts semantic polarity trends across Twitter, providing new evidence of how online audiences are shaped in their discourse by TV news language — an important link that prior research has not empirically established at-scale.

- Finally, we use model interpretation to extract lexical features from different entities, showing which words drive significant Granger-causal patterns in how broadcast media language shapes Twitter discourse and vice-versa, and thereby highlighting how language plays a key role in driving semantic polarity relations between online discussions and broadcast media language.

Our findings are among the first to quantify how language characterizing opposing media narratives about similar news events on TV can increase levels of partisan discourse online. The results lend support to recent communications scholarship, which theorizes that media and public agendas can influence each other, and that such dynamics can polarize the way the public engages in discourse, thereby influencing democratic decision-making at-large.
